# Reversing protonation of weakly basic drugs greatly enhances intracellular diffusion and decreases lysosomal sequestration ## Authors - Debabrata Dey1 ([ORCID: 0000-0003-3794-6476](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3794-6476)) - Shir Marciano1 - Anna Poryval2 - Ondřej Groborz2 - Lucie Wohlrabova2 - Tomás Slanina2 - Gideon Schreiber1 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-2922-5882](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2922-5882)) † ### Affiliations 1. Department of Biomolecular Sciences, Weizmann Institute of Science Rehovot Israel ([ROR:0316ej306](https://ror.org/0316ej306)) 2. Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry of the Czech Academy of Sciences Prague Czech Republic ([ROR:04nfjn472](https://ror.org/04nfjn472)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract For drugs to be active they have to reach their targets. Within cells this requires crossing the cell membrane, and then free diffusion, distribution, and availability. Here, we explored the in-cell diffusion rates and distribution of a series of small molecular fluorescent drugs, in comparison to proteins, by microscopy and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP). While all proteins diffused freely, we found a strong correlation between pKa and the intracellular diffusion and distribution of small molecule drugs. Weakly basic, small-molecule drugs displayed lower fractional recovery after photobleaching and 10- to-20-fold slower diffusion rates in cells than in aqueous solutions. As, more than half of pharmaceutical drugs are weakly basic, they, are protonated in the cell cytoplasm. Protonation, facilitates the formation of membrane impermeable ionic form of the weak base small molecules. This results in ion trapping, further reducing diffusion rates of weakly basic small molecule drugs under macromolecular crowding conditions where other nonspecific interactions become more relevant and dominant. Our imaging studies showed that acidic organelles, particularly the lysosome, captured these molecules. Surprisingly, blocking lysosomal import only slightly increased diffusion rates and fractional recovery. Conversely, blocking protonation by N-acetylated analogues, greatly enhanced their diffusion and fractional recovery after FRAP. Based on these results, N-acetylation of small molecule drugs may improve the intracellular availability and distribution of weakly basic, small molecule drugs within cells. ## Introduction Drug molecules alter many biochemical reaction pathways inside the cell by interacting with proteins, DNAs, RNAs, or others. By this, they influence one or more specific cellular activities (Ong et al., 2009; Schreiber, 2005; Stockwell, 2004). Due to their bioactivity, stability, rather simple chemical synthesis allowing for industrial bulk scale production and the easiness of administration, most drugs are small molecules (<1 kDa) (Ngo and Garneau-Tsodikova, 2018; Veber et al., 2002). Over half of these drugs have a significant degree of hydrophobicity and are weakly basic at intracellular pH of 7.4 (Charifson and Walters, 2014; Lipinski et al., 1997). Hydrophobicity is required to cross the lipid bilayer of the cell membranes, and polar functional groups solubilize the drug in the cellular medium (Lipinski et al., 1997). The balance between pKa and logP (partition coefficient of small molecules as measured from their partition between octanol/water) is critical for successful drug design (Manallack, 2007; Meanwell, 2011). Lipinski’s ‘Rules of 5’ suggests that logP should be between 1 and 6 to be a candidate for successful oral administration. Small molecule drugs can be acidic or basic depending on their pKa values (Lipinski et al., 1997). Drugs with pKa ~0–7 are considered acidic, and pKa ~8–14 are regarded as basic or alkaline. Basic drugs with pKa ˃8 are more common than their acidic counterparts (pKa ˂ 7, ~60:40 ratios). In some cases, lowering their pKa to the range between 6 and 7, has proven beneficial (Charifson and Walters, 2014). For a long time, mechanisms such as passive diffusion (Di et al., 2012) and carrier-mediated drug delivery (Dobson and Kell, 2008) or a combination of both Sugano et al., 2010 have been used to explain intracellular drug delivery. However, transport of a drug across the cellular membrane is only one part of a successful delivery. Intracellular diffusion and bio-distribution needs to be taken in account when assessing the drug mode of action. In previous work, we studied the diffusion of fluorescent drug molecules in crowded environments in vitro (Dey et al., 2022). However, the cellular cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells is by far more complex (Model et al., 2021). Intracellular membranes, multiple organelles (Ellis, 2001; Fulton, 1982) and a large diversity of macromolecules, in terms of size, charge and hydrophobicity, render the cellular interior extremely complex and heterogeneous (Milo and Phillips, 2015; Neurohr and Amon, 2020). Moreover, the pH inside cellular organelles can vastly differ from the cytosolic pH (Madshus, 1988). Organelles like lysosomes, late endosomes, Golgi, and secretory vesicles are acidic and have been known for sequestering weakly basic drugs (Asokan and Cho, 2002; Proksch, 2018). Therefore, predicting diffusion of a particular drug molecule in the dense cytoplasm is a complex task and requires sub-organelle resolution. For example, positively charged (basic) drugs designed to target nuclear DNA may bind cytoplasmic matter through nonspecific interactions (Long et al., 2022; Tiwari et al., 2018), they could be sequestrated within the lysosome, or diffuse slower than expected due to crowding and nonspecific interactions (Gotink et al., 2011; Jansen et al., 1999; Zhitomirsky and Assaraf, 2015). The mobility of a drug in the cellular interior has been shown to be a good proxy for intracellular drug delivery and other processes, such as nonspecific binding or aggregation (Dey et al., 2022). The primary tool for measuring small molecule diffusion inside the cell is fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), which inherently requires fluorescent drug molecules. FRAP with a confocal microscope is a sufficiently sensitive, versatile, and easy-to-use method suitable for measuring the diffusion of weakly fluorescent molecules. Unfortunately, single-molecule fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS), a gold-standard method for measuring diffusion of fluorescent particles, cannot be applied for most small molecule drugs due to their weak fluorescence (Dey et al., 2022; Dey et al., 2021; Zotter et al., 2017). In this work, we determined the intracellular diffusion coefficients of a series of fluorescent dyes and drugs compared to protein diffusion by FRAP (Figure 1 and Table 1). Specifically, we used Line-FRAP, which has a much higher time resolution and therefore can measure faster diffusion rates in comparison to standard FRAP (800 Hz versus 50 Hz), for detailed explanations, see Dey et al., 2022; Dey et al., 2021. A pictorial representation of Line FRAP performed in a live HeLa cell treated with a fluorescent drug is shown in Figure 2A. The small red circle denotes the bleached area which is done by using a Clip tornado (of 2x2 pixel size). The white line indicates the scanning region which was performed along at a rate of 800 Hz in order to record the FRAP as a function of time. The Line-FRAP cross-section profile as a function of time is shown in Figure 2B. The vertical direction of the line denotes the time progress. The vertically marked white rectangular region of interest (ROI), in the left panel (Figure 2B) shows the fluorescence intensity recovery over time, which is plotted in Figure 2C. The horizontal rectangular ROI outlined in white (in the right panel of Figure 2B) denotes the time frame immediately after the photo-bleach pulse (the highly intense green is the bleach pulse). The time interval between each line scanning measurement is ~1.25 ms. This horizontal white ROI generates the fluorescence intensity over the scanning line distance which is plotted in Figure 2D. This profile gives the effective bleach radius when fitted with a gaussian function (Dey et al., 2022; Dey et al., 2021). The apparent diffusion coefficients derived from FRAP measurements are termed Dconfocal are calculated using Equation 1: $$ D_{confocal}=\frac{r_{e}^{2}+r_{n}^{2}}{8\tau_{1/2}} $$ where t1/2 is the half-time of recovery and re and rn are the effective and nominal bleach radii values (for details see Dey et al., 2021). Dconfocal values for proteins determined by Line-FRAP agreed with the diffusion rates measured by FCS (Dey et al., 2021). For small molecules, Line-FRAP only provides relative 3D diffusion coefficients (Dey et al., 2022). We studied the following fluorescent drugs: the antimalarial drugs Quinacrine dihydrochloride (Ehsanian et al., 2011), primaquine phosphate (Camarda et al., 2019) and amidoquine (Olliaro and Mussano, 2003). The anti-cancer drug mitoxantrone (Shenkenberg and Hoff, 1986), and the glycogen synthase kinase GSK3 inhibitor SB216763 (Wagman et al., 2004). In addition, we monitored the diffusion of the diagnostic staining agent fluorescein disodium salt (Jampol and Cunha-Vaz, 1984), the fluorogenic substrate CCF2 (Zuverink and Barbieri, 2015) and boron dipyrromethene (BODIPY) analogues, which are used as fluorescent markers for lipids, membranes, and other lipophilic compounds (Poryvai et al., 2022). **Table 1.** LogP, pKa and lysosomal sequestration of drugs used in this study.(Predicted by ChemAxon software, and obtained from drug bank data base Zhitomirsky and Assaraf, 2015).

The diffusion coefficients and their cellular distributions showed very slow diffusion of the basic compounds, and low FRAP recovery, combined with an accumulation of the molecules in lysosomes. Surprisingly, while inhibiting the V-ATPase H+ pump using Bafilomycin A1 (Spugnini et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2021) or sodium azide (Hiruma et al., 2007) inhibited accumulation in lysosomes, cellular diffusion and fractional recovery increased only slightly. Contrary, blocking protonatable amino groups by acetylation greatly enhanced diffusion and FRAP recovery of studied small molecules. As over half the small molecule drugs are basic, our findings should be considered in drug assessment and development, as slow diffusion and low FRAP recovery is directly related to reduced cellular activity. Contrary to small molecules, we show here that diffusion rates within the cytoplasm of HeLa cells of 16 different E. coli proteins with pKa values of 4.5–8, are within the expected range, suggesting that hindered diffusion is mainly a problem of small molecules. ## Results ### Acidic proteins diffuse freely in the HeLa cytoplasm We have previously shown that diffusion in the cellular cytoplasm of E-fts and baeR, two bacterial globular proteins, aligns with the expected values considering the ~ two- to three fold higher macro-viscosity (Dey et al., 2021). Here, we extended this study to include 16 additional proteins (mostly from E. coli) whose oligomeric states in solution were previously characterized (Appendix 1—table 1 and Marciano et al., 2022). The aim was to determine how different heterologous proteins (E. coli proteins in HeLa cells) diffuse. The proteins showed Dconfocal values of 18–30 µm2s–1 in HeLa cell cytoplasm, which is typical for a cytoplasmic protein diffusion coefficient (Figure 2E). Moreover, full FRAP recovery was observed, indicating free diffusion. Appendix 1—table 1 provides the predicted isoelectric points and net charges at pH 7.4 of the purified proteins as calculated by Prot Pi, showing pKa values of 4.5–8, which are representative of the majority of E. coli cytosolic proteins. The results show that acidic and neutral proteins, even if not in their native environment, do not stick to the HeLa cell cytoplasm or membranes. ### Negatively charged small molecules rapidly diffuse in live cells Fluorescein is a negatively charged small organic molecule (pKa’s=2.85, 3.7, M.W.=332 Da, Figure 1 and Table 1). We showed in previous work that fluorescein diffusion is slower in the presence of crowder proteins like BSA, lysozyme and, myoglobin, even at relatively low protein concentrations (Dey et al., 2022). Here, the Fluorescein dye was micro-injected in live HeLa cells, followed by FRAP measurements (Figure 3A–D). We found that the diffusion coefficient of fluorescein in PBS (Dconfocal of 56.5±2.4 µm2s–1) was reduced to Dconfocal of 38.5±2.0 µm2s–1 in HeLa cytoplasm (Figure 3C). In the cell nucleus, a value of Dconfocal of 43.2±2.2 µm2s–1 was determined, while in concentrated HeLa cell extract (equivalent protein concentration of ~100 mg/mL), Dconfocal of 49.6±1.9 µm2s–1 was measured. The faster Dconfocal in cell extract compared to live-cell cytoplasm may result from the higher crowding density of the latter. The lowering of diffusion coefficients of negatively charged fluorescein correlates with the increasing crowding density of the medium moving from simple buffer to cells. For comparison, we also incubated HeLa cells for 24 hr with fluorescein, which is sufficient time for it to accumulate in the cells by diffusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B). While micrographs did not show dye aggregation inside the cell cytoplasm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B) and diffusion rates are similar to those determined by microinjection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), the fractional recovery dropped from 0.95 to 0.65. This suggests that a fraction of fluorescein is immobile in the cell after 24 hr incubation, and is not diffusing. ![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/97255/elife-97255-fig3-v1.jpg) **Figure 3.:** Comparative merged FRAP profiles (N=30; R=0.99 for each of the fits) in PBS and inside HeLa cells with exponential fits are shown for (A) Fluorescein, (E) CCF2 and (H) CF514. For calculating the Dconfocal values shown in Figure 3C, 30 individual Line-FRAP curves were merged for signal to noise reduction (Figure 3A; Dey et al., 2022; Dey et al., 2021). For comparison, we calculated Dconfocal values from individual Line FRAP progression curves in HeLa cytoplasm (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B), obtaining the same mean value as for the merged curve (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and D), however, with much larger variation over the mean. To estimate whether the large variation from the mean of the individual curves is due to different fluorescein concentrations in the individual measurements, we plotted the fluorescence signal (which is directly related to the concentration) versus the FRAP recovery rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, F) and versus the percent recovery (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G, H). The lack of correlation suggests that the variation in FRAP rates of the individual measurements is due to the low signal to noise of the individual curves versus the average. Next, we calculated Dconfocal also for fluorescein in PBS, nucleus and HeLa cell extract (Figure 3B). The mean values from individual curves are very similar to those calculated from the merged curves (Figure 3C), with a normal distribution of the individual calculated Dconfocal values around the mean. Moreover, also for the values measured in the nucleus, no relation between fluorescein concentration and FRAP rates or percent recovery was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F and H). Overall, this suggest that merged curves can be used to calculate Dconfocal values, as they give much better signal to noise, with apparent minimal loss of information. CCF2 is a fluorogenic substrate used for monitoring β-lactamase activity, with a pKa of ~5.1 (Zlokarnik et al., 1998). It is composed of cephalosporin core linking B7-hydroxycoumarin to fluorescein (Figure 1). Its calculated Dconfocal values in PBS and inside cells are about half as fast as those measured for fluorescein (Figure 3E–G), and its fractional recovery is ~0.7. No sign of aggregation is seen in micrographs inside the cell cytoplasm or nucleus (Figure 3G). The substantial slower rate of recovery, and lower fractional recovery of CCF2 relative to Fluorescein suggests its diffusion to be obstructed within the cell. This is in line with our prediction, that the observed substrate limited enzymatic degradation of CCF2 in HeLa cells is a consequence of its occlusion within the cellular cytoplasm (Zotter et al., 2017). A third molecule for which we determined the diffusion coefficient is the labelling dye CF514. It is used to label proteins and has high quantum yield. As its structure has not been published, we estimated the pKa value from the pH-dependent UV-spectrophotometry measurements. The sharp changes of the UV- spectrum at pH~3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, B), as well as the redshift confirms a pKa value of ~3. The FRAP curves look similar to fluorescein (Figure 3H–J), with ~90% recovery after FRAP. Dconfocal in PBS was ~61.1 ± 3.0 µm2s–1, and 26.3±1.9 and 29.2±2.0 µm2s–1 in the cell cytoplasm and nucleus of HeLa cells, respectively (Figure 3I). The drop of Dconfocal is attributed to cellular crowding. The results so far show that acidic small molecules diffuse well inside cells. Next, we focus on basic small molecules with higher pKa values. ### High FRAP recovery but slow diffusion measured for the glycogen synthase kinase (GSK3) inhibitor SB216763 The GSK3 inhibitor SB216763 (pKa = 7.0, M.W.=371 Da, Figure 1) aggregates when dissolved in PBS buffer solution. However, in our previous study we have seen that aggregation of this particular small molecule drug can be reversed by adding BSA and the extent of de-aggregation depends on the amount of BSA added (Dey et al., 2022). Here, our aim is to compare diffusion behavior of the GSK3 inhibitor in solution phase to that found in live cell cytoplasm. Since the molecule has some inherent solubility issues in PBS buffer, we compared its diffusion also in BSA protein solution and in cell culture media DMEM (Dulbecco’s modified eagle medium). Comparative FRAP profiles and Dconfocal rates of SB216763 in different mediums are shown in Figure 4A–C. The FRAP profiles and relative Dconfocal values show very slow diffusion of SB216763 in HeLa cell cytoplasm of ~0.61 ± 0.03 µm2s–1 with a fraction recovery of 0.8 after 10 s (Figure 4A–C). This is an ~40-fold reduction in Dconfocal compared to measurements in 50 mg/mL BSA protein solution, where SB216763 is not aggregating (Dconfocal~21.4 ± 0.5 µm2s–1 and fractional recovery of ~0.9 - Figure 4A–C). In cell culture DMEM media (containing 5% serum protein) fractional recovery after FRAP is very low (Figure 4A), indicating that the drug is still aggregating (Dey et al., 2022). Interestingly, the Dconfocal value in HeLa cell extract was higher ~11.3 ± 0.7 µm2s–1 as is its fractional recovery (0.9), showing that HeLa cell extract, like BSA is disaggregating SB216763. Co-localization with Lysotracker-633 (Figure 4D–E) shows that SB216763 colocalizes and is sequestered in acidic chambers of the cell lysosomes. Moreover, SB216763 accumulation into the lysosome increased over time (Figure 4D and E, 45-min and 2 hr treatment). Varying drug dosages resulted in Dconfocal values of 0.42–0.61 µm2s–1, suggesting that the slow diffusion is not related to SB216763 concentration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B). To validate Dconfocal values determined from merged progression curves, we calculated them also using individual Line FRAP profiles (Figure 4C vs 4B), with both methods showing the same mean values. Individual FRAP progression curves are shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, which have a much lower signal-to-noise ratio in HeLa cell cytoplasm, but result in a similar mean Dconfocal value as determined from the merged curves (Figure 4A-C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D). This rate dropped to Dconfocal~2.5 ± 0.1 µm2s–1 in HeLa cell cytoplasm, with fraction recovery of ~0.8, in comparison to one in buffer. In HeLa cell extract a Dconfocal rate of 15.1±0.6 µm2s–1 was determined, which lays between PBS and HeLa cytoplasm. Dconfocal estimated from individual Line FRAP profiles and the merged Line FRAP profile (Figure 5B vs 5 C) are also shown. Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D shows that the merged FRAP profile yields less noisy data and gives a better fit, yet the mean Dconfocal values are the same. As with SB216763, lower fraction recovery is observed at high Quinacrine concentrations, but the FRAP rates seem to be concentration independent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F). Micrographs of live HeLa cells show that the Quinacrine DHC molecules aggregate in the cytoplasm. Co-localization with Lysotracker-633 (Figure 5D, E) show that Quinacrine colocalizes and is sequestered in acidic chambers of the cell lysosomes. Moreover, Quinacrine aggregation into the lysosome increased over time (Figure 5D and E, 45-min and 2 hr treatment). Therefore, we measured diffusion instantaneously following micro-injection, and compared it to 2 and 24 hr of incubation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B). Quinacrine accumulation in the lysosome was observed also immediately after micro-injection, with aggregation increasing over time. Dconfocal of 4.2±0.2 µm2s–1 was calculated from line-FRAP immediately after micro-injection, slowing to 2.2±0.1 µm2s–1 following 2 hr incubations, with fractional recoveries of 0.63 and 0.57, respectively. After 24 hr of incubation the fractional recovery is less than 0.25, and thus the diffusion value is meaningless (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, D). Next, we compared FRAP of the cells treated with 2 and 6 µM Quinacrine solutions after 2- and 24 hr incubations (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–F). The concentration of Quinacrine had only a marginal effect on the results. Error bars represent SE calculated from fitting the FRAP progression curves, which are averaged over at least 30 independent measurements. ### Mitoxantrone, primaquine and amidoquine all aggregate within cells Mitoxantrone (anti-cancer) and primaquine phosphate (antimalarial) fluorescence show low quantum yields and weak photo-stability. However, due to their slow diffusion, the temporal resolution of standard XY-FRAP was sufficient for FRAP measurements (Figure 6A–H). Figure 6A and E show very low fraction recovery for these two drugs, suggesting that these weakly basic drugs are also sequestered in the cellular cytoplasm, as indeed shown in Figure 6B and F. The low pKa of weakly basic small molecule drugs drive their accumulation in the lysosome. There, they become protonated (ionic form is less-permeable), which hinders their back-diffusion to the cytosol. The phenomenon is known as cationic ion trapping (Asokan and Cho, 2002; Kaufmann and Krise, 2007) and results in drug accumulation in lysosomes up to millimolar concentrations (de Duve et al., 1974). We blocked lysosomal acidification using either Bafilomycin A1 or sodium azide (Figure 7) prior to drug administration. Bafilomycin A1 is a specific V-ATPase inhibitor and thus inhibits the supply of protons to the lysosomal chamber (Wang et al., 2021). Sodium azide, blocks ATP generation, resulting in the disruption of cellular activities which require ATP (Hiruma et al., 2007; Ishii et al., 2014). As a result, cationic ion trapping is inhibited. These two compounds were used to investigate whether lysosomal trapping is the cause for the 20- to 40-fold lower diffusion rates and lower fraction recovery in HeLa cells compared to buffer. All drug molecules used here are fluorescent, allowing for their FRAP measurements. Previously, we found that small-molecule drugs diffuse differently in crowded media than in a simple buffer solution, even if aggregation is not an issue (Dey et al., 2022). Here, we show that many small molecules get trapped within the cellular cytoplasm, resulting in extremely slow diffusion and lower fractional recovery after FRAP. This is particularly observed for cationic-charged small molecules, with Dconfocal values being 20- to 40-fold lower than observed for fluorescein or CF514 (Figure 9A vs 9B), which, in many cases is accompanied by low recovery after photobleaching. The later suggests that most molecules are occluded to components of the HeLa cell cytoplasm. Even dense cell extract from HeLa cells is not mimicking the in vivo results (Figures 4A–C–5A–C). This is very different from protein diffusion, where none of the 16 proteins measured here showed slow diffusion or low fractional recovery, despite their E. coli origin, expressed in HeLa cells. Slow diffusion and lower fractional recovery were limited to basic small molecules, showing Dconfocal values of 0.2–2 µm2s–1. While the fractional recovery for all proteins is ~0.9, for many basic small molecules it is 0.2–0.5. ![Figure 9.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/97255/elife-97255-fig9-v1.jpg) **Figure 9.:** Comparison of Dconfocal values of small molecule drugs in (A) PBS buffer and in (B) HeLa cells. (B) Dependency of Dconfocal on the number of aromatic rings in the drugs. As primary culprit for the slow diffusion of the basic small molecule drugs, we suspected sequestration in the lysosomes. Indeed, high level of accumulation in the lysosomes were found for all the basic drugs. However, pre-treatment with sodium azide or Bafilomycin A1, which we showed to inhibit lysosomal accumulation, had no or only a small effect on diffusion or fractional recovery after FRAP, which stayed low. Therefore, we evaluated colocalization of GSK3 inhibitor with lipid droplets, the ER or nucleic acids present in cytoplasm (Appendix 1—figures 1–3), but did not detect any. The conclusive evidence that slow diffusion and lower FRAP recovery results from the drugs being basic came by altering three molecules from being basic to acidic and vice versa. The best example here is fluorescein, where transformation to 5-amino fluorescein drastically reduced its diffusion as well as its fractional recovery after FRAP. Two additional examples here were Primaquine that was modified to Primaquine Acetate and BODIPY-NH2 that was modified to BODIPY-NHAc. In both cases, the diffusion became faster, and the fractional recovery increased significantly. We did not find any specific correlation between individual average diffusion rate constants with the concentration of small molecule drugs inside the cell (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E). For fraction recovery, we saw some decrease at high concentrations for the GSK3 inhibitor and Quinacrine, but not fluorescein (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), which would support our notion that they are sequestered in the cell. Correlating the calculated Dconfocal values with pKa shows a clear trend, where diffusion is strongly slowed down at higher pKa values (Figure 9C). Conversely, logP, molecular weights or number of aromatic rings present in the drug molecules did not relate to Dconfocal values (Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A, B). This finding is important, as the activity of a drug within the cell is dictated by its active concentration. When the drug is sequestered, its active concentration is reduced. Even, if it is not fully sequestered, but only diffuses much slower, it will result in lower association rate constant, and thus lower affinity towards the drug target. As a result, to keep the drug active, its dose has to be increased, which can have negative implications on side effects, due to off-target binding. ### Conclusions Our study shows that in vitro biophysical crowding studies for small molecule drugs are of limited value if one wants to understand the biophysical behavior of the same drug within the cell. While it is true that availability of a drug within a cell is only one factor dictating its biological activity, it is a crucial one. Our findings here raise an important limitation on the standard rules for drug design, as these do not consider the stickiness of basic small molecules within the cell. We were able to directly address this question by using fluorescent molecule drugs, and measuring their location and diffusion within cells. Most importantly, we also show that by blocking protonation of a number of basic compounds we were able to increase substantially their diffusion and recovery after photobleaching, and thus potentially their activity. These findings may be consequential in future drug development. ## Materials and methods All the reagents used are described in the Key Resources Table. When the areas of bleach were selected in the drug-treated cell cytoplasm, we avoided the lysosomes as much as possible, within the resolution limits of the confocal microscope. Lysosomes themselves were measured to move within the cytoplasm with an diffusion coefficient of 0.03–0.071 µm2 s−1 (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2014), which is much slower than the diffusion measured for even the slowest compounds using fast Line FRAP, further validating that we did not measure lysosome diffusion. ### Determination of Dconfocal from FRAP results We previously developed (Dey et al., 2021) the FRAP in Line mode (Line FRAP) method to monitor the diffusion rates of proteins in various environments. Line-FRAP allows a much faster data acquisition rate compared to classical XY FRAP. It is more suitable for measuring diffusion rates for fast diffusing molecules. To calculate Dconfocal, 20–30 independent measurements on different cells (n) were binned, and the curve fit of the progression curve was used to obtain t1/2, and re values and their associated errors as determined from the fit of the curve. rn was obtained from bleaching a fixed sample. The Dconfocal values were then calculated using Equation 1 (see ntroduction and Dey et al., 2021). The standard errors (SE) of the individual parameters were combined to obtain Dconfocal ± SE. The errors and means were used to calculate the significance level of the difference between two treatments, with ns for non-significant, * being for 0.05–0.01, ** being for 0.01–0.005, *** for 0.005–0.001 and ****<0.0001. Dconfocal values from individual Line FRAP profiles were calculated the same way, and one-way ANOVA statistical tests were performed to calculate the significance between treatments using the standard function available in GraphPad Prism v10.1 using Dunnett for multiple comparisons. To verify SE values, we repeated the ~20–30 measurements independently multiple times, which gave the same SE as obtained from individual curve fits of n=30 cells.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.97255.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.97255.3.sa1)

Summary:

The authors set out to measure the diffusion of small drug molecules inside live cells. To do this, they selected a range of fluorescent drugs, as well as some commonly used dyes, and used FRAP to quantify their diffusion. The authors find that drugs diffuse and localize within the cell in a way that is weakly correlated with their charge, with positively charged molecules displaying dramatically slower diffusion and a high degree of subcellular localization.

The study is important because it points to an important issue related to the way drugs behave inside cells beyond the simple "IC50" metric (a decidedly mesoscopic/systemic value). The authors conclude, and I agree, that their results point to nuanced effects that are governed by drug chemistry that could be optimized to make them more effective.

Strengths:

(1) The work examines an understudied aspect of drug delivery.

(2) The work uses well-established methodologies to measure diffusion in cells

(3) The work provides an extensive dataset, covering a range of chemistries that are common in small molecule drug design

(4) The authors consider several explanations as to the origin of changes in cellular diffusion

Comments on revised version:

In general, my comments were addressed, new discussions were added, and the paper has been improved significantly, which is great.

However, despite providing very clear instructions, a lot of my comments re statistical treatment were disregarded. Bar charts still do not show the repeats as individual points. Errors bars still represent SEM, which gives a wrong idea about the spread of the data. FRAP lines are still averages, and still do not show the spread of the data.

Significance assignments are done based on average and SEMs, as opposed to the full dataset. There is nothing technically wrong with this, but it generally creates an impression that things are more reproducible/rigorous/significant than they would be if the data was shown completely.

claims.claim: Hindered diffusion is mainly a problem of small molecules.
claims.source: Contrary to small molecules, we show here that diffusion rates within the cytoplasm of HeLa cells of 16 different E. coli proteins with pKa values of 4.5–8, are within the expected range, suggesting that hindered diffusion is mainly a problem of small molecules.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that proteins diffuse freely while basic small molecules do not.

results.result: E. coli proteins with pKa values of 4.5–8 diffuse freely in HeLa cell cytoplasm with Dconfocal values of 18–30 µm²s⁻¹ and full FRAP recovery, indicating that acidic and neutral proteins do not stick to HeLa cell cytoplasm or membranes even in a non-native environment.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by FRAP measurements on 16 E. coli proteins showing typical cytoplasmic diffusion coefficients and complete recovery. The pKa range (C3) is computationally predicted but reasonable. The conclusion (C4, C181) that hindered diffusion is mainly a problem for small molecules rather than proteins is supported by the contrast with basic drug behavior shown later.

results.result: Fluorescein (pKa ~3) shows reduced diffusion in HeLa cytoplasm (38.5±2.0 µm²s⁻¹) compared to PBS (56.5±2.4 µm²s⁻¹), with intermediate values in nucleus and cell extract. After 24 hr incubation, fractional recovery drops from 0.95 to 0.65, suggesting partial immobilization.
results.evaluation: The diffusion measurements (C5-C8) are well-documented with error bars. The correlation with crowding density (C10) is reasonable but somewhat speculative (C9). The 24 hr incubation result (C11-C12) is concerning as it suggests time-dependent changes that could complicate interpretation, but the observation is clearly documented.

results.result: CCF2 (pKa ~5.1) diffuses about half as fast as fluorescein with fractional recovery of ~0.7 and no visible aggregation, suggesting obstructed diffusion within cells that may explain substrate-limited enzymatic degradation.
results.evaluation: The pKa value (C13) is cited from literature. Diffusion measurements (C14-C15) are comparative and well-documented. The lack of aggregation (C16) is based on microscopy. The interpretation of obstructed diffusion (C17) is reasonable, and the connection to previous work on CCF2 degradation (C18) provides independent support.

results.result: CF514 (pKa ~3) shows similar behavior to fluorescein with ~90% FRAP recovery and diffusion rates of 61.1±3.0 µm²s⁻¹ in PBS and 26.3±1.9 µm²s⁻¹ in cytoplasm, supporting the conclusion that acidic small molecules diffuse well inside cells.
results.evaluation: The pKa determination from UV spectroscopy (C19) is appropriate. Diffusion measurements (C20-C22) are well-documented. The high recovery (C23) and attribution to crowding (C24) are consistent with fluorescein data. The summary conclusion (C25) is well-supported by the three acidic molecules studied.

results.result: GSK3 inhibitor SB216763 (pKa 7.0) shows very slow diffusion in HeLa cytoplasm (0.61±0.03 µm²s⁻¹) with ~40-fold reduction compared to BSA solution, colocalizes with lysosomes with time-dependent accumulation, and shows concentration-independent slow diffusion.
results.evaluation: The dramatic reduction in diffusion (C30-C32) is well-documented. The comparison with BSA solution (C33-C35) provides important context showing the drug doesn't aggregate in protein solution. Lysosomal colocalization (C41-C42) is demonstrated by microscopy. The concentration independence (C43-C44) strengthens the conclusion that slow diffusion is not due to self-aggregation at these concentrations.

results.result: Quinacrine DHC shows fast diffusion in PBS (41.9±3.0 µm²s⁻¹) but dramatically reduced diffusion in HeLa cytoplasm (2.5±0.1 µm²s⁻¹), with visible aggregation, lysosomal sequestration, and time-dependent decrease in diffusion and fractional recovery.
results.evaluation: The diffusion measurements (C46-C49) show dramatic differences between buffer and cells. Microscopy evidence of aggregation (C50) and lysosomal colocalization (C51-C52) is clear. The time-dependent changes (C54-C57) are particularly important, showing diffusion decreases from 4.2 to 2.2 µm²s⁻¹ over 2 hours and fractional recovery drops below 0.25 after 24 hours. This suggests progressive sequestration or aggregation.

results.result: Mitoxantrone and primaquine show low quantum yields, weak photostability, very low fractional recovery, and sequestration in cellular cytoplasm and lysosomes.
results.evaluation: The photophysical properties (C60) explain why standard XY-FRAP was used instead of Line-FRAP (C61). The low fractional recovery (C62) and sequestration (C63-C65) are documented by FRAP and colocalization microscopy. However, the inability to measure diffusion coefficients for these compounds limits quantitative comparison.

results.result: Lysosomal pH (~4.5) is maintained by V-H+-ATPase, and weakly basic drugs accumulate in lysosomes through cationic ion trapping, reaching millimolar concentrations. Bafilomycin A1 and sodium azide can inhibit this process.
results.evaluation: These claims (C66-C73) represent established knowledge from the literature and are appropriately cited. They provide the mechanistic framework for interpreting the experimental observations. The citations appear appropriate and the mechanisms are well-established in the field.

results.result: Bafilomycin A1 strongly reduces lysosomal volumes but does not significantly alter diffusion coefficients of GSK3 inhibitor (0.60±0.02 µm²s⁻¹) or Quinacrine (2.4±0.1 µm²s⁻¹), suggesting lysosomal accumulation is not the primary cause of slow diffusion. Time-dependent changes in Quinacrine diffusion support self-aggregation or aggregation with cellular molecules.
results.evaluation: This is a critical result. The microscopy clearly shows reduced lysosomal volumes (C74-C75), but diffusion rates remain slow (C76-C79). This surprising finding (C80) challenges the initial hypothesis that lysosomal sequestration explains slow diffusion. The time-dependent analysis (C81-C82) and interpretation (C83-C85) provide additional mechanistic insight, though the interpretation remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: Sodium azide inhibits lysosomal accumulation and causes modest further reductions in diffusion rates (Quinacrine: 2.4 to 1.8 µm²s⁻¹; GSK3 inhibitor: 0.6 to 0.45 µm²s⁻¹), with the difference from Bafilomycin possibly due to cytosolic acidification.
results.evaluation: The microscopy evidence (C86) and diffusion measurements (C87-C88) are clear. The observation that sodium azide causes a small decrease rather than increase in diffusion (unlike Bafilomycin) is interesting. The interpretation (C90) about cytosolic acidification is speculative but reasonable. Both treatments eliminate lysosomal confinement (C89), yet diffusion remains slow.

results.result: 5-amino fluorescein (pKa ~9) differs from fluorescein only by an -NH2 group but shows much slower FRAP recovery (0.4 vs complete) and lysosomal sequestration. Sodium azide alleviates sequestration but has minimal effect on FRAP, strongly suggesting the primary amine group is the main contributor to slow diffusion.
results.evaluation: This is an elegant experiment. The structural similarity (C91) makes this a near-perfect comparison. The dramatic difference in recovery (C92) and sequestration (C93-C94) is clear. The sodium azide experiment (C95-C96) is crucial: it eliminates lysosomal sequestration but doesn't restore fast diffusion, supporting the conclusion (C97) that the amine group itself causes slow diffusion through cytoplasmic interactions, not just lysosomal trapping.

results.result: N-acetylation of primary amines increases fractional recovery and diffusion: primaquine (0.27) vs primaquine-NHAc (0.6); BODIPY-NH2 (57%) vs BODIPY-NHAc (67%), with faster recovery half-life for acetylated forms.
results.evaluation: The chemical modification strategy is well-designed. The improvements in fractional recovery (C98-C101) and recovery kinetics (C102) are clearly documented. These results (C117-C118) provide strong support for the role of protonatable amines in causing slow diffusion and suggest a potential drug design strategy.

results.result: No colocalization was found between basic drugs and lipid droplets, ER, or cytoplasmic nucleic acids, leaving the location of cytoplasmic sequestration unidentified except for lysosomes.
results.evaluation: The negative results (C103-C105) are important to report and appropriately documented. The conclusion (C106) honestly acknowledges the limitation that the sequestration site remains unknown. This suggests the drugs may interact with multiple cellular components or form small aggregates below the resolution limit.

results.result: Many small molecules, particularly cationic ones, get trapped in cellular cytoplasm with extremely slow diffusion (0.2–2 µm²s⁻¹) and low fractional recovery (0.2–0.5), showing 20- to 40-fold lower Dconfocal than acidic molecules. This behavior is not mimicked by cell extract.
results.evaluation: This summary result integrates multiple observations. The quantitative comparisons (C109, C111, C113) are well-documented. The contrast with proteins (C112) is important. The observation that cell extract doesn't mimic in vivo behavior (C110) is a critical finding for the field, suggesting that simple crowding models are insufficient.

results.result: Pre-treatment with sodium azide or Bafilomycin A1 inhibits lysosomal accumulation but has minimal effect on diffusion or fractional recovery. In contrast, blocking protonation by N-acetylation greatly enhances diffusion and fractional recovery.
results.evaluation: This result synthesizes the key mechanistic findings. The lysosomal inhibitor experiments (C114-C115) show that lysosomal sequestration is not the primary cause of slow diffusion. The N-acetylation experiments (C116, C128, C137) demonstrate that protonatable groups are the key factor. This is the central mechanistic insight of the paper.

results.result: There is a strong correlation between pKa and intracellular diffusion, with diffusion strongly slowed at higher pKa values. LogP, molecular weight, and number of aromatic rings do not correlate with Dconfocal.
results.evaluation: The correlation analysis (C119, C179) is clearly shown in Figure 9C and represents a key finding. The lack of correlation with other properties (C120) strengthens the conclusion that pKa is the critical parameter. However, the correlation is based on a limited number of compounds, and the relationship appears non-linear, which could benefit from more detailed analysis.

results.result: Drug activity depends on active concentration, which is reduced by sequestration. Slow diffusion lowers association rate constants and affinity, requiring higher doses with potential off-target effects. Standard drug design rules don't consider intracellular stickiness of basic molecules.
results.evaluation: These claims (C121-C127) represent logical inferences about the implications of the findings. The reasoning is sound: slow diffusion and sequestration will affect drug-target interactions kinetically and thermodynamically. The critique of current drug design practices (C127) is justified by the data. However, these are implications rather than directly tested hypotheses.

results.result: Blocking protonation potentially increases drug activity, and N-acetylation may improve intracellular availability and distribution of weakly basic drugs, with potential consequences for future drug development.
results.evaluation: While the diffusion and FRAP data (C128, C137) clearly show improved mobility with N-acetylation, the claims about increased activity (C129) and improved drug performance (C138) are speculative. No actual drug activity assays are presented. The potential for drug development (C130) is reasonable but would require extensive additional work including activity assays, pharmacokinetics, and toxicity studies.

results.result: Over half of pharmaceutical drugs are weakly basic and protonated at physiological pH, facilitating membrane-impermeable ionic forms and ion trapping. The cellular cytoplasm is complex with varying pH in organelles, making drug diffusion prediction challenging and requiring consideration of intracellular distribution.
results.evaluation: These claims (C131-C159) represent established knowledge from the literature and provide important context. They are appropriately cited and accurately represent current understanding of drug properties, cellular complexity, and drug distribution challenges. This background justifies the importance of the current study.

results.result: Drug mobility is a good proxy for intracellular delivery. FRAP is suitable for weakly fluorescent molecules, while FCS cannot be applied to most drugs. Line-FRAP has higher temporal resolution (800 Hz vs 50 Hz) and measures faster diffusion than standard FRAP, with validation against FCS for proteins.
results.evaluation: The methodological claims are well-supported by citations to previous work (C160, C162-C166). The technical specifications (C163-C164) are clearly stated. The validation against FCS (C165) is important. The limitation for small molecules (C166) is honestly acknowledged. These claims establish the appropriateness of the methodology.

results.result: The drugs studied include antimalarials (quinacrine, primaquine, amodiaquine), anti-cancer (mitoxantrone), GSK3 inhibitor (SB216763), diagnostic agents (fluorescein), and fluorescent markers (CCF2, BODIPY). Lysosome diffusion (0.03–0.071 µm²s⁻¹) is much slower than measured drug diffusion, validating that FRAP doesn't measure lysosome movement.
results.evaluation: These claims establish the identity and properties of the compounds studied (C167-C174) with appropriate citations. The comparison with lysosome diffusion rates (C175-C176) is important for validating that the FRAP measurements reflect drug diffusion rather than organelle movement. This is a critical control.

results.result: Weakly basic small-molecule drugs display 10- to 20-fold slower diffusion rates and lower fractional recovery in cells compared to aqueous solutions.
results.evaluation: This summary claim is well-supported by the extensive FRAP data throughout the manuscript comparing buffer and cellular measurements. The quantitative range (10- to 20-fold) is consistent with the specific measurements reported for individual drugs. This represents a key finding of the study.

results.result: The authors measured diffusion of 16 E. coli proteins (pKa 4.5–8) in HeLa cells using FRAP and found Dconfocal values of 18–30 µm²s⁻¹ with full recovery, indicating free diffusion. They conclude that acidic and neutral proteins do not stick to HeLa cell cytoplasm or membranes even in a non-native environment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the protein diffusion measurements. The editor's summary describes the data as 'convincing' and the study as 'valuable,' and reviewers praised the 'extensive dataset' and 'well-established methodologies.' The protein data serve as a control showing normal diffusion behavior.

results.result: The authors measured diffusion of acidic small molecules (fluorescein, CCF2, CF514) in various environments. Fluorescein showed Dconfocal of 56.5±2.4 µm²s⁻¹ in PBS, 38.5±2.0 µm²s⁻¹ in HeLa cytoplasm, 43.2±2.2 µm²s⁻¹ in nucleus, and 49.6±1.9 µm²s⁻¹ in cell extract. Similar patterns were observed for CCF2 and CF514. The authors conclude that acidic small molecules diffuse well inside cells, with reduced rates attributed to cellular crowding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these measurements without specific critique. The editor noted the data are 'convincing' regarding how 'diffusion behavior depends on their charged state.' One reviewer acknowledged the work 'provides an extensive dataset' using 'well-established methodologies.' The acidic molecule data establish the baseline for comparison with basic drugs.

results.result: The authors measured GSK3 inhibitor SB216763 (pKa=7.0) diffusion showing very slow Dconfocal of ~0.61±0.03 µm²s⁻¹ in HeLa cytoplasm (~40-fold slower than in BSA solution) with fractional recovery of 0.8. Microscopy showed colocalization with lysosomes that increased over time. The authors report 10- to 20-fold slower diffusion rates for weakly basic drugs in cells than in aqueous solutions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these core findings. The editor's summary states the study presents 'convincing data indicating that their diffusion behavior depends on their charged state.' Reviewers noted the work 'points to an important issue' and provides 'an extensive dataset.' The dramatic slowing of basic drug diffusion is a central finding that reviewers did not challenge.

results.result: The authors measured Quinacrine DHC diffusion showing Dconfocal of 41.9±3.0 µm²s⁻¹ in PBS but only ~2.5±0.1 µm²s⁻¹ in HeLa cytoplasm with fractional recovery ~0.8. Microscopy showed aggregation and lysosomal sequestration increasing over time. Immediately after microinjection, Dconfocal was 4.2±0.2 µm²s⁻¹, slowing to 2.2±0.1 µm²s⁻¹ after 2 hr and <0.25 fractional recovery after 24 hr.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these measurements. The editor noted the data are 'convincing' and reviewers praised the 'extensive dataset' and methodology. The time-dependent changes in Quinacrine diffusion support the authors' interpretation of progressive sequestration and/or aggregation, which reviewers accepted as part of the overall findings.

results.result: The authors measured mitoxantrone and primaquine showing very low fractional recovery and sequestration in cellular cytoplasm. Colocalization studies confirmed primaquine and amodiaquine are sequestered in lysosomes. Despite low quantum yields and weak photo-stability, standard XY-FRAP was sufficient due to slow diffusion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings without specific critique. The measurements are consistent with the overall pattern for weakly basic drugs. Reviewers noted the work 'provides an extensive dataset, covering a range of chemistries that are common in small molecule drug design,' implicitly accepting these additional examples.

results.result: The authors tested whether lysosomal sequestration explains slow diffusion by treating cells with Bafilomycin A1 or sodium azide. Both treatments strongly reduced lysosomal volumes and drug accumulation, but had no or only small effects on diffusion rates (GSK3 inhibitor: 0.60±0.02 µm²s⁻¹; Quinacrine: 2.4±0.1 µm²s⁻¹ after Bafilomycin). The authors conclude lysosomal accumulation is not the primary reason for slow cytoplasmic diffusion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this surprising finding. The editor's summary notes the study proposes 'that blocking drug protonation enhances diffusion and fractional recovery,' acknowledging the mechanistic experiments. One reviewer stated the authors 'consider several explanations as to the origin of changes in cellular diffusion,' indicating acceptance of this experimental approach and interpretation.

results.result: The authors tested the role of protonation by comparing fluorescein (pKa~3) to 5-amino fluorescein (pKa~9). The amino derivative showed much slower recovery (fractional recovery 0.4 vs. complete for fluorescein) and lysosomal sequestration. Sodium azide treatment alleviated sequestration but had only small effects on FRAP. The authors conclude the primary amine group is the main contributor to slow diffusion and low recovery.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly endorsed this experiment. The editor's summary highlights that the study 'proposes that blocking drug protonation enhances diffusion and fractional recovery, suggesting improved intracellular availability of weakly basic drugs.' One reviewer specifically praised 'Altering a compound's pKa value and measuring cytosolic diffusion rates' as 'certainly inciteful' and 'demonstrated relevance to drug targeting and drug development.'

results.result: The authors tested N-acetylation to block protonation in primaquine and BODIPY-NH2. Primaquine-NHAc showed fractional recovery of ~0.6 vs. ~0.27 for primaquine. BODIPY-NHAc showed ~67% recovery vs. ~57% for BODIPY-NH2, with faster recovery half-life. The authors conclude blocking protonation substantially increases diffusion and fractional recovery.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly supported these findings. The editor's summary emphasizes 'blocking drug protonation enhances diffusion and fractional recovery.' One reviewer stated this experiment 'demonstrated relevance to drug targeting and drug development' and another noted the authors 'adequately corrected the errors, added new information and data based off the reviewers suggestions that improved the manuscript.'

results.result: The authors correlated diffusion coefficients with molecular properties and found a clear trend where diffusion is strongly slowed at higher pKa values. In contrast, logP, molecular weight, and number of aromatic rings did not correlate with Dconfocal values. The authors conclude there is a strong correlation between pKa and intracellular diffusion and distribution.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this correlation analysis. The editor's summary states the data are 'convincing' that 'diffusion behavior depends on their charged state.' One reviewer noted the work examines 'an understudied aspect of drug delivery' and 'points to nuanced effects that are governed by drug chemistry,' implicitly accepting the pKa correlation as the key chemical property.

results.result: The authors conclude that many small molecules get trapped in cellular cytoplasm with extremely slow diffusion (0.2–2 µm²s⁻¹) and low fractional recovery (0.2–0.5), particularly for cationic-charged molecules (20- to 40-fold slower than acidic molecules). Cell extract does not mimic in vivo results. The authors argue standard drug design rules do not consider this stickiness, and N-acetylation may improve intracellular availability of weakly basic drugs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers endorsed these conclusions. The editor's summary states the findings are 'significant for drug design and understanding the biophysical behavior of small molecules in cells.' One reviewer noted the work 'points to an important issue' and 'their results point to nuanced effects that are governed by drug chemistry that could be optimized to make them more effective.' Another stated the manuscript 'would add quality information to a part of the literature that is lacking much needed information.'

results.result: The authors tested colocalization of drugs with lipid droplets, ER, and nucleic acids but found no colocalization. They conclude they could not pinpoint the location of sequestration within the cellular cytoplasm except for the lysosome.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these negative results. One reviewer noted the authors 'consider several explanations as to the origin of changes in cellular diffusion,' indicating acceptance of the comprehensive approach including negative findings. These results support the conclusion that mechanisms beyond simple organelle sequestration are involved.

results.result: The authors measured CCF2 (pKa~5.1) showing diffusion rates about half as fast as fluorescein with fractional recovery ~0.7 and no visible aggregation. They interpret the slower recovery and lower fractional recovery as suggesting obstructed diffusion, consistent with their prediction that substrate-limited enzymatic degradation of CCF2 results from occlusion within the cellular cytoplasm.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these CCF2 measurements or interpretations. The data fit the overall pattern of charge-dependent diffusion. The connection to previous work on enzymatic degradation was accepted as part of the broader narrative about how diffusion affects drug function.

results.result: The authors report that GSK3 inhibitor SB216763 (pKa=7.0) aggregates in PBS buffer but this aggregation can be reversed by adding BSA, with the extent of de-aggregation depending on BSA amount, citing their previous work.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these background observations about aggregation in buffer. This contextualizes the in-cell measurements and explains why BSA solution was used as a control condition. The citation to previous work was accepted.

results.result: The authors provide extensive background on drug properties, ion trapping mechanisms, cellular complexity, and established principles of drug design including Lipinski's Rules of 5, pKa ranges, and the prevalence of weakly basic drugs (~60% of drugs have pKa>8).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this background material, which represents established knowledge properly cited from the literature. One reviewer noted 'The manuscript was fairly well written,' indicating acceptance of how the background contextualizes the findings.

results.result: The authors describe their Line-FRAP methodology, noting it has higher temporal resolution than standard FRAP (800 Hz vs. 50 Hz), can measure faster diffusion rates, and has been validated against FCS for proteins. They note FCS cannot be applied to most small molecule drugs due to weak fluorescence, but Line-FRAP only provides relative 3D diffusion coefficients for small molecules.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised significant concerns about statistical presentation and data display. One reviewer stated 'despite providing very clear instructions, a lot of my comments re statistical treatment were disregarded. Bar charts still do not show the repeats as individual points. Errors bars still represent SEM, which gives a wrong idea about the spread of the data. FRAP lines are still averages, and still do not show the spread of the data.' This suggests methodological concerns about data presentation, though not about the fundamental validity of the Line-FRAP approach itself.

results.result: The authors discuss implications: drug activity depends on active concentration, sequestration reduces this, slow diffusion lowers association rate constants and affinity, requiring higher doses with potential side effects. They speculate that blocking protonation potentially increases activity and findings may be consequential for future drug development.
results.evaluation: Reviewers endorsed these implications. The editor noted the findings are 'significant for drug design.' One reviewer stated the work 'points to nuanced effects that are governed by drug chemistry that could be optimized to make them more effective' and another noted the experiment 'demonstrated relevance to drug targeting and drug development.' The speculative nature of some statements (e.g., 'potentially,' 'may be') is appropriate for discussion.
